findings.trigger: The module-level import at :53-57 wraps `from services.infrastructure.action_logger import log_user_action, _ACTION_LOG_FILE as ACTION_LOG_FILE` in `try/except ImportError`, falling back to `from app.utils.web_helpers import ACTION_LOG_FILE, log_user_action`. This is exactly the anti-pattern the comment two lines above (14-24) says was just removed for `rate_limit`, with the same reasoning stated there: 'an except ImportError around a module that DOES exist would also swallow an ImportError raised inside [it] itself, and a broken dependency there would quietly become "use the fallback" with nobody told'. If `services.infrastructure.action_logger` exists but a transitive import inside it breaks (e.g. a refactor elsewhere), this second try/except silently swallows that and switches `get_action_log` (which reads `ACTION_LOG_FILE` at :68) to the `app.utils.web_helpers` fallback path with no error surfaced anywhere.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same fix already applied to `rate_limit`: import `services.infrastructure.action_logger` unconditionally (or catch a narrower, explicitly-checked condition such as `ModuleNotFoundError` for the module itself, not for anything inside it), so a broken dependency inside the central module is not mistaken for 'central module not present'.
findings.unsure_why: Cannot see app/utils/web_helpers.py from this section, so I cannot tell whether its ACTION_LOG_FILE/log_user_action are equivalent to the canonical ones (making the fallback merely silent-but-harmless) or materially different/stale (making it a Z3/Z8-style wrong-result-reported-as-fine case). Either way the silent swallow itself is visible in the given source.

findings.trigger: `download_action_log` (:84-92) wraps `send_file(ACTION_LOG_FILE, ...)` in a `try` that only catches `FileNotFoundError`. Its sibling `get_action_log` (:64-80), reading the same file two routes above, explicitly separates out `(IOError, OSError, PermissionError)` and `(UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError)` as distinct, expected failure modes. `PermissionError` is a sibling of `FileNotFoundError` under `OSError`, not a subclass of it, so if the action log file exists but cannot be read (permission denied, or another OSError such as a device/I-O error), `send_file` raises unhandled here: the user gets Flask's generic error page instead of the friendly `flash(...)` + redirect the route is clearly meant to give for exactly this class of problem.
findings.suggestion: Give `download_action_log` the same `(IOError, OSError, PermissionError)` except arm as `get_action_log`, flashing an equivalent message instead of letting it propagate.

findings.trigger: `game_query_support_status` (:601-613) has no `try/except` at all - the only route in this file without one. Its own docstring says it is 'polled by the UI during a manual test'. If `read_support_verdicts()` (:606-607) raises - e.g. the verdicts file is corrupted or mid-write - the exception propagates unhandled, so the polling request gets Flask's default error response instead of the `{'container':..., 'supported':..., ...}` JSON shape every other endpoint in this file falls back to on error.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the body in the same `(ImportError, AttributeError, RuntimeError)` / `(ValueError, TypeError, KeyError)` pattern used by every other route in this file, returning a JSON error body so the polling frontend can handle it instead of failing to parse a non-JSON response.
findings.unsure_why: Whether the Flask app registers a global JSON error handler that would convert an uncaught exception here into a JSON response anyway is not visible in this section's source; if it does, the practical impact is smaller than a raw HTML 500 to a JS poller.

findings.trigger: In `add_task` (:91-94) and identically in the PUT branch of `edit_task_route` (:338-341), `_player_warnings(result.task_data)` is called twice: once for the `if` truthiness check and again to build the value stored under `answer['warnings']`. `_player_warnings` (:32-49) calls `services.scheduling.player_gate.query_problems(...)`, code not in this section, on every call. If that call is not perfectly deterministic between two back-to-back invocations with the same arguments (e.g. it re-checks live container/query state rather than only the just-saved task data), the boolean that gates whether a warning is shown and the list actually shown can disagree - and either way the check work (and any I/O `query_problems` does) runs twice for no functional reason, doubling the added latency of every task add/edit that waits for an empty server.
findings.suggestion: Call `_player_warnings(result.task_data)` once, store it in a local variable, and use that variable both for the truthiness check and for `answer['warnings']`, in both `add_task` and `edit_task_route`.
findings.unsure_why: services/scheduling/player_gate.py is not part of this review section, so I cannot confirm whether query_problems is a pure/deterministic check (making this only wasted work) or has state/timing sensitivity (making the two calls able to disagree).

notes: Several places in main_routes.py already carry explicit in-code review annotations (review D8, D9, D24, D25, D29, D30) documenting prior findings and, in most cases, their fixes (e.g. setup_save now catches ConfigServiceError per D25; get_mech_display_info no longer returns cache_directory per D8; the is_active bool coercion fix per D29). These are not re-reported as new findings here since the code and comments show them already handled/decided. One of them, D24 on game_query_retest (:554), documents that a RuntimeError from a failed thread start is not listed in that route's except clause; I did not re-flag it separately because the comment shows the important guarantee (clearing the 'testing' spinner flag) is handled defensively via `except BaseException` before the re-raise - the remaining gap is only the HTTP response shape, already acknowledged in-code. I also checked whether get_donation_status (:384, no @auth.login_required) is a gap versus Z5/B2, but it is a read-only status endpoint consistent with other unauthenticated read-only endpoints in the same file (mech music/display info, which are documented at :1188 as deliberately public for Discord's credential-less fetches), so I did not treat it as a finding.
